title: Modi Demands End to Terror Double Standards at SCO Summit in Bishkek
excerpt: At the 26th SCO Summit in Kyrgyzstan, PM Modi called for dismantling the entire ecosystem of terrorism while sharing warm exchanges with Xi Jinping and Putin — as Pakistan's Sharif stood by without interaction.
body:
• Prime Minister Modi told the SCO Summit that terrorism "cannot be a strategic asset for anyone" and demanded the dismantling of its entire ecosystem, including financing, recruitment, and safe havens
  • Modi laid out three pillars for India's SCO engagement — Security, Connectivity, and Opportunity — while insisting that connectivity projects must respect national sovereignty, an implicit pushback against China's Belt and Road Initiative
  • The summit's optics were striking: Modi shared warm exchanges with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin, while Pakistan's Shehbaz Sharif stood nearby with no interaction
  • Pakistan assumes the rotating SCO chairmanship next and will host the 2027 summit, setting up a diplomatically charged year ahead

Prime Minister Narendra Modi used his address at the 26th Shanghai Cooperation Organisation summit in Bishkek on Monday to deliver a forceful call against terrorism, targeting what India considers Pakistan's use of militant proxies — without naming Islamabad directly.

"The entire ecosystem of terrorism — financing, recruitment, radicalisation, and safe havens — must be dismantled," Modi told leaders of the ten-member bloc. "Terrorism cannot be a strategic asset for anyone. There can be no double standards."

Three Pillars and a Sovereignty Red Line

Modi outlined India's framework for the SCO around three pillars: Security, Connectivity, and Opportunity. On connectivity, he stressed that infrastructure projects must respect national sovereignty and territorial integrity — a pointed reference to the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC), which passes through Pakistan-administered Kashmir that India claims.

On security, Modi called for a unified approach to combating radicalisation and cross-border terrorism, framing it as a prerequisite for regional stability. He announced that India will host the first session of the SCO Civilisational Dialogue Forum and highlighted India-led initiatives including a Start-up Forum, Young Authors' Conclave, and Young Scientists' Forum.

Wars and West Asia

Addressing the conflicts roiling multiple regions, Modi called for dialogue over battlefield resolutions — a message with clear implications for the Russia-Ukraine war, now grinding through its fourth year. He stopped short of criticising Russia, a close defence partner, but said India would continue supporting all peace efforts.

On West Asia, Modi warned that the ongoing crisis was disrupting energy security, maritime trade routes, and global supply chains, urging collective action through the SCO framework. He also reaffirmed India's commitment to development and humanitarian assistance in Afghanistan.

The Photo-Op That Spoke Volumes

The summit's most closely watched moments played out in front of cameras rather than behind microphones. Modi shared a warm handshake with Chinese President Xi Jinping and gave Russian President Vladimir Putin a friendly pat on the back — a visual signal of diplomatic thaw with Beijing and continued closeness with Moscow.

Pakistan's Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, standing nearby beside Putin, had no visible exchange with Modi. The contrast underscored the frozen state of India-Pakistan relations, which deteriorated sharply after the Pahalgam attack earlier this year.

Pakistan's Turn at the Helm

Pakistan assumes the rotating SCO chairmanship next and will host the 2027 summit. The handover creates an awkward diplomatic dynamic: India will need to navigate engagement with the bloc under Pakistani stewardship while bilateral ties remain near historic lows.

The SCO now comprises ten members — Belarus, China, India, Iran, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Pakistan, Russia, Tajikistan, and Uzbekistan — along with two observer states and fifteen dialogue partners. Despite its expanding membership, the bloc's internal fault lines were on full display in Bishkek, with India and Pakistan on opposing sides of the terrorism debate and China and India sparring over sovereignty-linked infrastructure.

For the Indian diaspora, Modi's terrorism stance carries particular weight in the post-Pahalgam environment, where India-Pakistan tensions have reshaped everything from visa policies to cricket scheduling. The SCO remains one of the few multilateral stages where the two nuclear neighbours share a table.
